A uniform field meets a slab of material at an angle: which way do its lines turn?

Listen to the intro

About: the bending of E and B field lines at the faces of a slab of linear material

About this simulation

On screen
A slab seen edge-on as a pale grey band between its two faces, which run off both sides. Blue field lines with arrowheads arrive from above at β0 to the dashed vertical normal, run on inside the slab at β and leave below. In the electric view, lines that stop at the upper face end on minus signs of bound charge, and new lines start on plus signs at the lower face; the magnetic view has no signs. In the magnetic view, circled dots on the upper face and circled crosses on the lower face mark the bound surface currents (out of and into the page) that strengthen the part of B along the faces. Arcs mark β0 above the face and β just inside it. Where the centre line enters, amber arrows split the applied field (solid) into its part along the face and its part along the normal (dashed), and do the same for the field just inside, on one scale: E∥ is kept and E⊥ is divided by εr; B⊥ is kept and B∥ is multiplied by μr. The slab is taken to be infinitely wide.
Readouts
In the sidebar under Controls: β0; inside the slab β, the field as a fraction of the applied field and the share of lines that pass the upper face; and below the slab the angle and field again.
Controls
Field chooses the electric view (a dielectric of relative permittivity εr) or the magnetic view (a magnetic material of relative permeability μr). β0 sets the angle of the applied field to the normal, 0° to 80°. The εr / μr slider sets the material, 1.0 to 10, and keeps its value when the view is switched. The picture is static and redrawn at once.
Measured
β, the field inside as a fraction of the applied field and the field below the slab come from the engine's boundary operations at the upper and lower faces, with an applied field of size 1. Outside the slab the lines are a tenth of the view width apart; inside they are spaced so that the number crossing unit length of a face follows the normal component.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Into a dielectric slab

Choose the electric view, set β0 to 45° and keep εr at 1.0. You will raise εr to 4.0. Before you do, predict how the lines inside the slab will change direction.

2 · Out through the lower face

Keep β0 at 45° and εr at 4.0. Before looking below the slab, predict the direction of the lines after they leave through the lower face.

3 · A quarter of the lines, 0.73 of the field

Keep β0 at 45° and εr at 4.0, and count the lines at the upper face: only one line in four carries on into the slab, and the rest end on the minus signs. Yet the readout gives the field inside as 0.73 of the applied field, not 0.25. What explains the 0.73?

4 · Straight along the normal

Keep εr at 4.0 and set β0 to 0°, so that the applied field is along the normal. Before you do, predict the direction and the size of the field inside the slab.

5 · The magnetic view

Choose the magnetic view, set β0 to 45° and set μr to 4.0. Before you do, predict what the lines of B do at the faces.

6 · Raise the permeability

Keep the magnetic view and β0 at 45°, and raise μr to 10. Before you do, predict what the lines inside the slab and below it do.

7 · What you found

E view: the part of E along a face and the normal part of D carry across unchanged, so tan β = εr tan β0. Inside, the lines tilt away from the normal and weaken, and a share 1 − 1/εr of them end on bound charge.

B view: the normal part of B and the part of H along a face carry across, so tan β = μr tan β0 too, but every line runs on and the field inside is stronger.

Below the slab the applied field is restored in both views.

Field Lines Crossing a Slab

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A uniform applied field meets a flat slab of linear material at an angle β0 to the normal. The sim draws the lines of the field above, inside and below the slab and reads out the angle and strength of the field on each side. It has an electric view (dielectric, relative permittivity εr) and a magnetic view (magnetic material, relative permeability μr).

What you'll learn

  • How the field splits into a part along a face and a part along its normal.
  • What fixes the angle β inside the slab.
  • What happens to the lines at the faces, in the electric and the magnetic views.
  • How strong the field is inside the slab.
The set-up: a slab with two faces, the normal n̂, and the applied field at β0.

What's on screen

  • Blue lines with arrowheads: the field, a tenth of the view width apart outside the slab.
  • Pale grey band: the slab seen edge-on. The dashed vertical line is the normal n̂, and arcs mark β0 above the upper face and β just inside it.
  • Amber arrows, where the centre line enters: the applied field (solid) and its two parts (dashed), then the same for the field just inside, on one scale.
  • Signs on the faces: in the electric view − and + mark bound charge, and in the magnetic view circled dots and crosses mark bound surface currents.
  • Readouts: β0 above the slab; then β, the field fraction and the share of lines passing inside; then the angle and field below.

03

E along a face is kept and E normal to it is divided by εr

Split the applied field Ea into the part Ea∥ along the faces and the part Ea⊥ along the normal. The tangential part of E is continuous across an interface (notes, eq. 8.34). The bound charge on the faces has a field along the normal, which cancels outside the slab and adds inside, so the field outside is Ea. Inside (notes, eqs. 8.41 and 8.42):

Here εr = 1 + χe. The second form says that the normal part of D is continuous.
The sim's amber arrows at the upper face. The part along the face is kept, and the normal part is divided by εr.

With Ea = 1, β0 = 45° and εr = 4, both parts of the applied field are 0.707. Inside, E∥ is still 0.707 and E⊥ = 0.707/4 = 0.177.

Key idea. At the faces only the part of E along the normal changes.
See itLook at the amber arrows at the upper face with εr = 4 and β0 = 45°. Watch for: the arrows just above the face with equal parts along the face and along the normal, and just inside it with the same part along the face and a normal part a quarter as long.
04

The lines tilt away from the normal: tan β = εr tan β0

The angle β of the field inside is set by the ratio of its two parts (notes, eq. 8.43):

The tilt of the lines inside the slab.

A line of E that passes from empty space into a dielectric with εr > 1 bends away from the normal, towards the faces (notes, p. 223). At β0 = 45° and εr = 4, tan β = 4 and β = 76°. With εr = 1 the faces do nothing, and β = β0.

β against β0. Every curve with εr > 1 lies above the diagonal, εr = 1.

At β0 = 45°, εr = 1.5, 3 and 10 give β = 56.3°, 71.6° and 84.3°. At β0 = 0° there is no part along the faces, and β stays 0°, but at εr = 4 a step to β0 = 5° already gives β = 19.3°.

Key idea. The larger εr, the closer to the faces the lines inside run.
See itRaise εr from 1 to 4 at β0 = 45°. Watch for: the lines inside the slab swinging from 45° to 76° towards the faces, with β in the Readouts following.
05

The lower face undoes the bend

At the lower face the field passes from the slab back into empty space, so equation (8.40) of the notes applies again with the two media swapped:

Here εr1 = εr is the slab and εr2 = 1 is the space below.

It gives tan β2 = tan β/εr = tan β0. The field below the slab is the applied field again, at the angle β0 and with the same strength. The bound charges on the two faces are equal and opposite, so outside the slab their fields cancel (notes, p. 223).

Lines of E for εr = 4 and β0 = 45°: 45° above, 76° inside, 45° below.

In the sim the readouts under Below the slab show 45° and 1.00 at εr = 4.

Key idea. The two faces together leave the field outside the slab as it was.
See itLook below the slab at εr = 4 and β0 = 45°. Watch for: the lines below the slab parallel to the lines above, with Angle to normal 45° and Field / applied 1.00 under Below the slab.
06

Lines of E end on bound charge, and the field is not Ea/εr

The normal part inside is Ea⊥/εr. In the sim the number of lines crossing a unit length of a face follows that part, so a share 1/εr of the lines arriving at the upper face carries on. The rest end on the negative bound charge of that face, and new lines begin on the positive bound charge of the lower face (notes, Figure 89a). At εr = 4 the share passing is 0.25. The size of the field inside includes the part along the faces:

The magnitude of E inside, from the two parts of the applied field.

At β0 = 45° and εr = 4 it is 0.729 Ea, not 0.25 Ea. Along the face the lines that carry on are 4 times as far apart as above the slab. Measured across the lines they are 1.37 times as far apart, and 1/1.37 = 0.73.

At β0 = 0° the field inside is Ea/εr = 0.25 Ea, as in a filled capacitor with its free charge held fixed. For a field along the faces there is no bound charge and the field inside is Ea (notes, p. 225).

Key idea. Ea/εr is right only for β0 = 0°.
See itRead the field inside at εr = 4 and β0 = 45°. Watch for: Field / applied 0.73 and Share of lines passing 0.25 inside the slab.
See itSet the applied field along the normal, with εr = 4. Watch for: no tilt, with β = 0°, and Field / applied 0.25.
07

Lines of B bend in the same way, and none of them end

For B the normal part is continuous, and the part along the faces is multiplied by μr, since B∥/μr is continuous (notes, eq. 8.39). The bound surface currents on the faces produce the jump, drawn in the sim as circled dots and crosses.

The jump in the part along the faces.
The same tilt as for E, with μr in place of εr (notes, p. 224), and the magnitude from the two parts.

There is no magnetic charge, so every line of B runs on through both faces and the share passing is 1.00. Inside the slab the lines lie closer together. At β0 = 45° and μr = 4, β = 76° and B/Ba = 2.92. At μr = 10, β = 84.3° and B/Ba = 7.11, with the lines nearly along the faces. Below the slab the lines leave at 45° again.

The field inside as a fraction of the applied field, with the material at 4. At β0 = 0° E is a quarter and B is 1.
Key idea. E weakens inside the slab and B strengthens, and the lines of both tilt towards the faces.
See itSwitch to the magnetic view at β0 = 45° with μr = 4. Watch for: every line running through both faces, β = 76°, Field / applied 2.92 and Share of lines passing 1.00.
See itRaise μr from 4 to 10 in the magnetic view. Watch for: the lines inside the slab lying nearly along the faces and crowding together, with β = 84° and Field / applied 7.11.
08

Summary

In one line. A uniform field crossing a slab is split into a part along the faces and a part along the normal, and the sim shows how the angle, the strength and the lines of the field change at the faces, in the electric and the magnetic views.
  • E∥ is kept and E⊥ = Ea⊥/εr (eq. 8.42), so tan β = εr tan β0 (eq. 8.43): 76° at 45° and εr = 4.
  • The lower face restores the applied field: β0 and the same strength below the slab.
  • A share 1/εr of the lines of E carries on, and the field inside is 0.73 Ea at 45°.
  • For B every line passes, B∥ is multiplied by μr, tan β = μr tan β0, and B/Ba = 2.92.

Common mix-ups

  • "A larger εr pulls the lines toward the normal." The normal part shrinks, so they move out to 76°.
  • "The field inside is Ea/εr at every angle." That holds only at β0 = 0°. At 45° it is 0.73 Ea.
  • "The lines below the slab stay tilted." The lower face undoes the upper one: 45° again, at the strength of Ea.
  • "Lines of B end on the faces, like lines of E." There is no magnetic charge, and every line passes.

Things to try on your own

  • At εr = 4, step β0 from 0° to 5° and read β.
  • Compare E and B at β0 = 80° with the material at 10.
